checks.title: Intune compliance rate at target
remediation: Set the target in the profile.

Work the noncompliant list: fix the device, retire it, or correct the compliance policy that is wrong. Compliance feeds Conditional Access (CA-005), so every noncompliant device is either blocked or, if the policy is not enforced yet, unprotected.

userImpact.text: Owners of noncompliant devices are asked to update, encrypt or re-enroll them, and may be blocked until they do.

checks.narrative: The compliance rate is the fraction of managed devices meeting the policy: encrypted, current, protected, healthy. It is what the compliant-device Conditional Access control enforces, so the number is both a hygiene measure and the size of the population a device-based policy would lock out. The per-platform split is in the facts.

checks.title: No stale Entra devices, or a cleanup rule is on
remediation: Enable the Intune device cleanup rule (DEV-013) at 90 days or less.
Clean up the stale Entra device objects listed once: disable them first and delete after a grace period.

userImpact.text: Stale devices nobody uses are removed; active devices are not touched.

checks.narrative: A device object that has not signed in for months still satisfies device-based Conditional Access if someone can use its credential, and it inflates every device count the report relies on. Stale objects are the inventory debt that makes join-type and compliance numbers unreliable.

checks.title: Join type mix: hybrid share within target
remediation: Set the target in the profile as the Entra-join migration progresses.
New and refreshed devices should be Entra joined with Autopilot; hybrid join stays only for devices that need on-premises resources the cloud cannot yet provide.

userImpact.text: New and reset devices join Entra directly; users sign in the same way.

checks.narrative: Entra joined, hybrid joined and registered devices get different controls and different attack surfaces. The mix is reported here so the trend is visible across runs; the threshold lets a migration set its own pace.

checks.title: Autopilot share of the Windows fleet at target
remediation: Register new hardware with Autopilot at purchase through the OEM or reseller.
Import the hardware hashes of existing devices due a reset.
Set the target in the profile for the refresh cycle.

userImpact.text: New devices set themselves up from the box when the user signs in, instead of arriving imaged.

checks.narrative: Autopilot-provisioned devices arrive Entra joined, enrolled and policy-bound before a user touches them. The share of the Windows fleet that came through Autopilot is a proxy for how much of it was built to the standard rather than migrated into it.

checks.title: BitLocker recovery keys escrowed for every Windows device
remediation: Deploy an Intune disk encryption policy with silent enablement and recovery key backup to Entra for all Windows devices.
Confirm the devices listed have escrowed a key. Devices encrypted before the policy may need the key backed up again with manage-bde or a remediation script.

userImpact.text: Encryption and key backup happen silently in the background.

checks.narrative: A Windows device without an escrowed recovery key is either unencrypted or encrypted with a key nobody holds, and the difference only shows up when the disk needs recovering. Key presence in Entra is the one signal that both encryption happened and the organisation can get the data back.

checks.title: FileVault enabled on every managed Mac
remediation: Deploy an Intune FileVault disk encryption policy with personal recovery key escrow and rotation after reveal.
Require encryption in the macOS compliance policy. Escrow state per Mac is not in the device record; (verify) the encryption report once the Intune reports collector exists.

userImpact.text: Mac users are asked once to turn on FileVault and restart.

checks.narrative: A lost MacBook without FileVault is a readable disk. Intune reports whether each managed Mac is encrypted; escrow of the recovery key is the second half, so that a locked-out user does not become a wiped machine.

checks.title: No Windows 10 devices left in the fleet
remediation: Size the refresh with the Windows build summary.
Upgrade or replace the devices listed. Windows 10 reached end of support in October 2025; a device still on it needs Extended Security Updates or it is unpatched.

userImpact.text: Users on Windows 10 get an upgraded or replaced device, with the downtime that brings.

checks.narrative: An unsupported operating system gets no security fixes. Every Windows 10 device without ESU is a known-vulnerable endpoint on the network, and the count is the first thing an auditor or an insurer asks about.

checks.title: Apple push certificate and VPP tokens well before expiry
remediation: Renew the Apple push certificate with the same Apple ID it was created with. A different ID means re-enrolling every Apple device.
Renew the VPP tokens in Apple Business Manager.
Put both expiry dates in the team calendar with a 60-day reminder.

userImpact.text: An admin renewal users never see, as long as it is done before the date.

checks.narrative: When the Apple push certificate lapses, every iPhone, iPad and Mac silently stops receiving management. If it is renewed with a different Apple ID, all of them must be re-enrolled by hand. It expires yearly and the person who created it has often left.

checks.title: Personal Windows devices blocked from enrollment
checks.remediation: In Intune enrollment device platform restrictions, block personally owned Windows devices in the default restriction, and only allow them for a named group if the BYOD stance in the profile changes to MDM.

userImpact.text: Users can no longer enroll a personal Windows PC; they use a company device or the web apps.

checks.narrative: With personal Windows enrollment open, anyone with a work account can enroll their home PC, which then counts as managed, may satisfy compliance, and pulls corporate data onto hardware nobody controls. The restriction keeps the managed fleet the organisation's own.

checks.title: Endpoint security policies present and assigned
checks.remediation: Create and assign an Intune endpoint security policy for each missing type: antivirus, disk encryption, firewall, attack surface reduction rules, and endpoint detection and response. Start from Microsoft's recommended settings and assign to all devices by platform.

userImpact.text: Users may see firewall or antivirus prompts the first time; most protections run silently.

checks.narrative: The five endpoint security policy types are how Intune tells devices to run Defender properly, encrypt the disk, keep the firewall on, block the common attack techniques and report to Defender for Endpoint. A missing type means that control is whatever the device defaulted to.

checks.title: Windows LAPS policy assigned
remediation: Enable Windows LAPS in Entra device settings.

Assign an Intune account protection policy for Local admin password solution to all Windows devices: back up to Entra, rotate after use, 30-day maximum age. (verify) the template display name matched by the fact.

userImpact.text: The local admin password is managed in the background.

checks.narrative: Without LAPS every Windows device shares the same local administrator password, or has one nobody knows. Either way a single compromised machine gives lateral movement to all of them. LAPS makes each password unique, rotated and retrievable only through an audited read.

checks.title: Defender for Endpoint connector enabled in Intune
remediation: In Intune endpoint security, open the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint connector and enable the connection for Windows and macOS (and Linux where managed).
Turn on compliance policy evaluation on device risk.
Enable the Intune connection in the Defender portal too.

userImpact.text: An admin connection users never see.

checks.narrative: The connector is what lets Intune onboard devices to Defender for Endpoint automatically and use device risk in compliance. Without it, onboarding is manual and a device under attack still reports compliant.

checks.title: Device cleanup rule enabled
checks.remediation: In Intune devices, device cleanup rules, enable the rule and set the inactivity period to 90 days or less so retired and forgotten devices leave the console on their own.

userImpact.text: Devices inactive for months leave the console; active devices are not touched.

checks.narrative: Without a cleanup rule, every device that was ever enrolled stays in the console, and the compliance and encryption percentages drift toward meaningless. The rule is a one-time setting that keeps the inventory honest.

checks.title: Linux endpoints enrolled in Intune
remediation: Enroll supported Linux desktops in Intune and deploy Defender for Endpoint on Linux through it.
Set a target count in the profile.
Where enrollment is not possible, record the alternative management in the profile so the gap is documented rather than invisible.

userImpact.text: Linux users enroll their device and get Defender installed.

checks.narrative: Linux desktops are usually the developers' machines with the most access and the least management. The count enrolled is reported here because zero is the common answer, and at scale zero is a finding.

checks.title: Compliance policies require a Defender device risk level
remediation: Turn on the Defender for Endpoint connector in Intune with compliance policy evaluation for each platform (DEV-012).
In each platform's assigned compliance policy, open Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and set Require the device to be at or under the machine risk score to Low or Clear.
Set the policy's actions for noncompliance to mark the device noncompliant immediately, then watch the compliance report for a day before relying on it.

userImpact.text: A device with an active threat loses access to Microsoft 365 until it is cleaned; users of healthy devices notice nothing.

checks.narrative: Defender for Endpoint scores each device's risk from what it sees on the machine. A compliance policy can require that score to be Low or Clear, which is how an attack in progress cuts the device off from Microsoft 365 until it is cleaned up. The setting is per platform and off by default.

checks.title: Personal phones and Macs enrol only when the BYOD stance allows it
remediation: In Intune, Devices, Enrollment, Device platform restriction, block personally owned devices for each platform listed in the default restriction.
Protect company data on personal phones with app protection policies instead (EP-018), which needs no enrollment.
If personal devices should enrol, set the profile's BYOD stance to mdm so this check agrees.

userImpact.text: People can no longer enrol a personal phone or Mac; they use app protection in Outlook and Teams on their own phone instead.

checks.narrative: Enrolling a personal device gives the organisation management of hardware it does not own and the person a reason to object, while the device still counts as managed for Conditional Access. Where the stance is app protection, personal enrollment should be closed so the two do not mix.

checks.title: Devices with no compliance policy count as noncompliant
remediation: In Intune, Devices, Compliance, Compliance settings, set Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as to Not compliant.
First check every platform in use has an assigned compliance policy, or those devices lose access (CA-005).

userImpact.text: Devices that no compliance policy covers lose access to company data until one does; covered devices notice nothing.

checks.narrative: With the default setting, a device that no compliance policy targets reports compliant, so Conditional Access that requires a compliant device lets it in without any check. Marking it noncompliant makes compliance mean something.

checks.title: Group Policy analysed for the move to Intune
remediation: Export the GPOs that apply to workstations from Group Policy Management as XML (Save Report).
In Intune, Devices, Group Policy analytics, import them and read which settings have an MDM equivalent.
Migrate the supported settings into settings catalog profiles, starting with the GPOs closest to 100 percent, and retire each GPO once its devices are covered.

userImpact.text: Analysis only; nothing changes for people until settings move to Intune.

checks.narrative: Moving devices from hybrid join to Entra join depends on replacing Group Policy with Intune. Group Policy analytics shows, GPO by GPO, which settings have an MDM equivalent, so the move can be planned rather than discovered when a setting goes missing.

checks.title: No Windows devices managed by Configuration Manager alone
remediation: Turn on co-management in Configuration Manager (Cloud Attach) for these devices, with automatic enrollment in Intune.
Move the compliance policies workload to Intune first, so Conditional Access gets a compliance signal, then device configuration, Windows Update policies and endpoint protection (DEV-021).
Build new and reset devices with Autopilot and Entra join, so they start in Intune and never need Configuration Manager.

userImpact.text: Devices enrol in Intune in the background; people see the Company Portal app and, later, Intune prompts such as Windows Hello set-up.

checks.narrative: A Windows device that Configuration Manager manages and Intune only sees through tenant attach has no Intune compliance state, so a Conditional Access policy that requires a compliant device cannot trust it. Intune's security baselines, Windows Hello cloud trust, remote actions over the internet and Autopilot reset do not reach it either. Co-management is the step between: Configuration Manager keeps what it does while Intune adds compliance and, workload by workload, takes over.

checks.title: Hybrid-joined Windows devices managed by Intune, not by Group Policy alone
remediation: Enrol hybrid-joined devices in Intune automatically: the Group Policy setting Enable automatic MDM enrollment using default Microsoft Entra credentials, or co-management where Configuration Manager is in use.
Check Group Policy analytics (DEV-018) for the settings Intune has to take over before any GPO is unlinked.
Plan the move to Entra join: new devices through Autopilot, existing ones at refresh, so the device no longer depends on a domain controller for policy.

userImpact.text: Devices enrol in the background and pick up Intune policies; people may see a restart, Windows Hello set-up and new apps arriving from the Company Portal.

checks.narrative: These Windows devices are joined to Active Directory and nothing in the cloud manages them: some are registered in Entra but not enrolled in Intune, and, with the AD collector's files, some are not registered in Entra at all. Group Policy, or Configuration Manager without tenant attach, is all they get. They report no compliance, so Conditional Access either blocks them or, more often, a policy leaves them out. Patching, encryption and Defender settings depend on the device reaching a domain controller over the office network or a VPN, and a lost laptop cannot be wiped from the cloud. Managed by Intune, people also gain self-service apps, updates wherever they work and Windows Hello sign-in.

checks.title: Co-management workloads moved to Intune
remediation: In Configuration Manager, Cloud Attach, Workloads, move Compliance policies to Intune: Pilot Intune for a test collection first, then Intune.
Then move Device configuration, Windows Update policies and Endpoint Protection the same way, each through the pilot collection.
Keep Client apps and Office Click-to-Run on Configuration Manager only while packages are still deployed from it, and plan their move too.

userImpact.text: Little changes for people: the same settings arrive from Intune instead of Configuration Manager, and update deadlines and restart notices follow the Intune update rings.

checks.narrative: Co-management only helps once workloads move. With compliance policies on Intune, Conditional Access gets a device signal; with device configuration, Windows Update policies and endpoint protection on Intune, settings and updates reach devices over the internet without a line of sight to a site server. Each workload moved is one less thing that needs the on-premises infrastructure.

checks.title: Macs on a partner MDM report compliance to Intune
remediation: In Intune, Tenant administration, Connectors and tokens, Partner compliance management, add the partner for macOS and assign the user groups whose Macs it manages.
In the partner's console (in Jamf Pro: Settings, Global, Device Compliance), connect it to Microsoft Entra ID and Intune for this tenant and confirm the connection.
Check that the heartbeat stays recent: a link that stops reporting marks its Macs noncompliant after the grace period, and Conditional Access then blocks them.

userImpact.text: People register their Mac once through the partner's app (Jamf Self Service, with the Company Portal); after that, signing in works as before.

checks.narrative: When Jamf or another Mac MDM manages the Macs, Intune knows whether a Mac is compliant only if the partner reports it. Without that link, a Conditional Access policy that requires a compliant device blocks every Mac, so in practice Macs end up excluded and sign in from anywhere with no device check. A partner that was connected and whose heartbeat stopped is the same gap, a few days later.

checks.title: Macs managed by a partner show as compliant in Entra
remediation: In the partner's console, look at the Macs reported noncompliant or not registered, and the compliance rules applied to them.
Have people whose Mac shows as not registered finish device registration from the partner's Self Service app.
Keep the Intune compliance policy for macOS assigned to the same users the partner reports for, so the partner's answer is what Conditional Access sees.

userImpact.text: People with a noncompliant or unregistered Mac are asked to fix or register it; everyone else sees nothing.

checks.narrative: A connected partner is only useful if the Macs it manages come through as compliant. A Mac that Entra lists as not compliant is blocked by a compliant-device policy, or pushes the organisation to loosen the policy; a Mac that never registered gets no device check at all.

checks.title: Every Intune certificate connector is connected
remediation: On each server listed, check that the Intune certificate connector services are running and that the server can reach Intune.
Look at the connector's event log (Applications and Services Logs, Microsoft, Intune, CertificateConnectors) for why it stopped.
Sign the connector in again or reinstall it, and remove from Intune any connector whose server is gone.

userImpact.text: While a connector is down no device gets a new or renewed certificate, so Wi-Fi, VPN and email that sign in with one stop working as certificates run out.

checks.narrative: The certificate connector is a Windows server on the network that hands certificates from the organisation's own certificate authority to Intune devices. Nothing in the cloud says when it stops, and the first sign is a device that cannot join the Wi-Fi weeks later. A connector Intune calls inactive, or one not heard from for days, is listed. A tenant with no connector passes: there is nothing to lose.

checks.title: Multi-admin approval protects changes that reach every device
remediation: Intune admin center, Tenant administration, Multi Admin Approval, Access policies: create a policy.
Start with the profile types that can do the most harm at once: device actions such as wipe and retire, scripts, and role changes.
Name an approver group of at least two people who are not the only ones who make such changes, so a request is never waiting on its own author.

userImpact.text: None for users. An admin who starts a protected change waits for a second admin to approve it.

checks.narrative: One Intune administrator session can wipe every device, or push a script to every device, in a few clicks. Attackers who take such a session have done exactly that. With multi-admin approval, a protected change one administrator starts does nothing until a second administrator approves it. The check passes when at least one approval policy exists, and the facts say which kinds of change the policies cover.

checks.title: No Intune role that can change things is assigned over every device and user
remediation: For each assignment listed, decide which devices and users that team really looks after.
Edit the assignment in Intune admin center, Tenant administration, Roles: set its scope to the groups it should reach, and use scope tags so the team sees only its own policies and apps.
Leave tenant-wide administration to the few people who hold the Intune Administrator role in Entra, activated through PIM.

userImpact.text: None for users. A help desk team whose assignment is narrowed stops seeing devices outside its groups.

checks.narrative: Intune has its own roles beside the Entra ones, and each assignment says which devices and users it reaches. An assignment over all devices and all users gives a team, often the help desk, the same reach as a tenant administrator for whatever the role allows: wiping, retiring, reading recovery keys. A read-only role is not listed, and a tenant that uses no Intune role assignments passes.
